title.en: History: The Beginning of the Modern Age

text.en: Raju compared two diagrams of early European sea voyages. He asked which waters each ship crossed and what people already lived along those routes.

The Renaissance was a broad renewal of art and learning in parts of Europe, beginning especially in Italian centres. The early modern period also involved religious, political and economic changes. Artists like Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo and thinkers like Galileo changed how people saw the world.
Gutenberg helped develop a system of movable metal type printing in fifteenth-century Europe. Printing histories in East Asia began earlier. Martin Luther became a major figure in the Protestant Reformation. It included several movements that challenged aspects of the Roman Catholic Church. Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492. Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498 by sailing around southern Africa. Both destinations had existing societies and trade.
The new sea routes opened trade and led to colonies. European ocean voyages expanded trade and helped build colonial empires. Indigenous communities experienced displacement, forced labour and disease, alongside changes in exchange and power.

board.text: Renaissance

text.en: The beginning of the modern age is a chapter label for several connected changes. The timing differs across regions and across activities such as trade, artistic work or religious reform.

board.text: Read period labels together with place and subject

text.en: Italian cities such as Florence and Venice had trade, workshops and wealthy patrons. Patrons helped fund some art and scholarship, and cities became centres for exchanging ideas.

board.text: Trade, workshops and patronage supported new work

text.en: Renaissance scholars studied Greek and Roman texts and adapted older ideas to new questions. The circulation of manuscripts and contact among scholars helped this work.

board.text: Renewed study of older sources

text.en: Humanist study often emphasised languages, history, rhetoric and moral questions. Its scholars used close reading and compared different versions of a text.

board.text: Humanism included close study of texts

text.en: Artists used techniques such as linear perspective to suggest depth on a flat surface. Compare lines in a painting to see how they can guide the viewer toward a single point.

board.text: Perspective can suggest depth

text.en: Leonardo studied art and the natural world, while Michelangelo worked in painting, sculpture and architecture. Their work shows how activities could overlap in Renaissance workshops.

board.text: Arts and inquiry could overlap

text.en: Printing with reusable type allowed printers to produce many copies. As copies circulated, more readers could compare the same text. Access still depended on language, cost and literacy.

board.text: Reproduction widened circulation

text.en: In the developing study of nature, observation and mathematical reasoning could challenge earlier explanations. Galileo’s telescope observations gave evidence for reconsidering some familiar accounts of the sky.

board.text: Observation can test an explanation

text.en: The Reformation addressed religious beliefs and practices, including questions of authority. Luther criticised the sale of indulgences and his arguments circulated in print.

board.text: Luther’s arguments circulated through print

text.en: Different reformers established different movements. Political rulers and local communities responded in different ways, so there was no single Protestant experience.

board.text: Reform varied across regions and institutions

text.en: The Roman Catholic Church pursued its own reforms. The Council of Trent restated doctrines and addressed questions of discipline. This is part of what the textbook calls the Counter-Reformation.

board.text: Catholic reforms included the Council of Trent

text.en: The Society of Jesus helped expand Catholic education and missions. These developments illustrate one institutional response to religious change.

board.text: Education and missions were part of Catholic reform

text.en: European merchants and rulers sought access to valuable goods and trade routes. Navigation, ship design and geographical knowledge helped make some longer voyages possible.

board.text: Trade aims and navigation knowledge supported voyages

text.en: Sailors could use a compass for direction and compare their position with charts or observations of the sky. A single instrument did not tell them an entire route.

board.text: Navigation used several kinds of evidence

text.en: Portuguese sailors explored routes along the west coast of Africa. Reaching the Indian Ocean around southern Africa brought them into routes used by established traders.

board.text: New to European sailors did not mean new to the region

text.en: Columbus sailed west seeking a route toward Asia. His voyage reached the Caribbean. People with their own societies had lived in the Americas long before this voyage.

board.text: Destination reached differed from destination sought

text.en: Da Gama reached Calicut in 1498. Read that voyage in the setting of existing Indian Ocean exchange, with merchants linking several ports and regions.

board.text: Calicut was part of existing maritime networks

text.en: The expedition begun by Magellan completed a voyage around the world under Elcano after Magellan died. Distinguish who started the expedition from who completed it.

board.text: Magellan began the voyage · Elcano completed it

text.en: Maritime links moved goods, crops and people between continents. Some movement was voluntary and some forced. Trade and conquest had different consequences for different communities.

board.text: Exchange included both voluntary and forced movement

text.en: Colonial settlement often changed control of land, labour and resources. Enslaved people and Indigenous communities experienced severe harm. Look for their perspectives alongside records written by colonisers.

board.text: Compare whose accounts are preserved

text.en: Overseas trade helped make some Atlantic ports more important. Earlier Mediterranean and Indian Ocean routes continued to matter. Old and new networks could operate together.

board.text: Trade patterns changed without replacing all older routes

text.en: A map can show route endpoints, but it cannot by itself show why sailors travelled or what happened after arrival. Pair it with an account or material evidence.

board.text: Maps and other sources answer different questions

text.en: Compare the chapter’s changes using a cause and an effect. Printing, religious reform and ocean voyages took place in overlapping centuries, but they did not all have one cause.

board.text: Separate a chronology from a causal claim

problem.en: Compare the routes of Columbus and da Gama. What can you infer from the routes alone?

text.en: Identify each departure region, route and endpoint.

why.en: Columbus crossed the Atlantic to the Caribbean. Da Gama reached India via southern Africa.

text.en: Separate the route evidence from wider historical claims.

why.en: The diagrams help compare journeys. Other sources are needed to study the effects of arrival.

prompt.en: A friend says Vasco da Gama reached America. How will you reply?
